title: The fundamental theorem proved
objectives: Prove the fundamental theorem of calculus.

screens.title: Area so far, and a thin strip
screens.prose: The blue area is $F(x) = \int_0^x t^2\,dt$, the area so far. The strip from $x$ to $x + h$ is what $F$ gains as $x$ moves on by $h$. Move $x$ and $h$, and watch the strip's area divided by $h$.
screens.question: At $x = 1.5$, what value does the strip's area over $h$ approach as $h$ shrinks?

hints.text: Set $h$ to 0.01 and read the caption.
The strip is nearly a rectangle of height $f(1.5)$ and width $h$.
So the area over $h$ approaches $1.5^2$.

feedback.correct: Right. The strip over $h$ tends to $f(1.5) = 2.25$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shrink $h$ and see where the caption settles.

byKey.h01: That is the value at $h = 0.1$. Shrink $h$ further: the ratio keeps falling towards the height.
byKey.F: You gave the area so far, $F(1.5) = 1.125$. The question is about the strip over $h$.

explain.text: The strip is almost a rectangle of height $f(x)$, so its area over $h$ tends to $f(1.5) = 2.25$. At $h = 0.1$ it is 2.4033 and at $h = 0.01$ it is 2.2650. So the slope of the area so far is the height of the curve: $F'(x) = f(x)$.

screens.title: The area so far cannot jump
screens.prose: Let $f$ be integrable on $[a, b]$ with $|f(t)| \le M$ for all $t$, and let $F(x) = \int_a^x f$. We call $F$ the **accumulation function**. For $y < x$ in $[a, b]$, $F(x) - F(y) = \int_y^x f$.

state.caption: The strip fits in a box of height $M$ and width $x - y$.

screens.question: Why is $F$ continuous, even where $f$ is not?

options.text: $|F(x) - F(y)| = \left|\int_y^x f\right|$, which is at most $M|x - y|$, small when $x$ is near $y$.
$F$ is differentiable, and differentiable functions are continuous.
options.why: That uses part one, which needs $f$ continuous. Here $f$ is only integrable, so it may jump.

options.text: $F$ has no jumps because $f$ has none.
options.why: You assumed $f$ is continuous. The bound uses only $|f| \le M$.

options.text: $F$ is an antiderivative of $f$, so it is smooth.
options.why: An antiderivative needs $F' = f$ everywhere, which can fail where $f$ jumps.

hints.text: Bound the strip's area by a rectangle.
The strip has width $x - y$ and lies between heights $-M$ and $M$.
So $|F(x) - F(y)| \le M|x - y|$; take $\delta = \tfrac{\varepsilon}{M}$.

feedback.correct: Right. $F$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$, so it is continuous.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use only the bound $|f| \le M$ and the width of the strip.

explain.text: $-M \le f \le M$ on $[y, x]$ gives $|\int_y^x f| \le M(x - y)$. So $|x - y| < \tfrac{\varepsilon}{M}$ forces $|F(x) - F(y)| < \varepsilon$. Here $M = 4$, and $F(1.6) - F(1.2) \approx 0.7893$ is below $4 \times 0.4 = 1.6$.

screens.title: The quotient minus the height
screens.prose: Now let $f$ be continuous at $c$. For $h \ne 0$, write $f(c) = \tfrac1h\int_c^{c+h} f(c)\,dt$. Then $$\frac{F(c+h) - F(c)}{h} - f(c) = \frac1h\int_c^{c+h}\big(f(t) - f(c)\big)\,dt.$$
screens.question: Why is the right side at most $\sup\{|f(t) - f(c)| : |t - c| \le |h|\}$ in size?

options.text: Call that supremum $s$. The integrand is at most $s$ in size over a length $|h|$. So the integral is at most $s|h|$; divide by $|h|$.
By the mean value theorem, $F(c + h) - F(c) = F'(\xi)\,h$.
options.why: That assumes $F$ is differentiable, which is what we are proving.

options.text: Because $f$ is constant near $c$.
options.why: Nothing says $f$ is constant. The bound uses only how far $f(t)$ is from $f(c)$.

options.text: Because $F$ is continuous at $c$.
options.why: Continuity of $F$ makes the top of the quotient small, but the bottom $h$ is small too.

hints.text: Bound the integrand first.
Each $t$ between $c$ and $c + h$ has $|t - c| \le |h|$.
So $|f(t) - f(c)| \le s$, and the integral is at most $s|h|$.

feedback.correct: Right. Size of the integrand times the length, over $|h|$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Bound $|f(t) - f(c)|$ on the strip, then use the strip's length $|h|$.

explain.text: For $t$ between $c$ and $c + h$, $|f(t) - f(c)| \le s$. The integral over a length $|h|$ is then at most $s|h|$ in size. Dividing by $|h|$ leaves $s$.

screens.title: Why the gap closes
screens.prose: So $\left|\tfrac{F(c+h) - F(c)}{h} - f(c)\right| \le s(h)$, where $s(h)$ is the supremum of $|f(t) - f(c)|$ for $|t - c| \le |h|$.
screens.question: Why does $s(h) \to 0$ as $h \to 0$?

options.text: $f$ is continuous at $c$: for $\varepsilon > 0$ some $\delta$ has $|f(t) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ when $|t - c| < \delta$, so $s(h) \le \varepsilon$ for $|h| < \delta$.
$f$ is integrable, so $s(h) \to 0$.
options.why: Integrable functions can jump. At a jump, $s(h)$ never falls below half the jump's size.

options.text: $F$ is continuous, so $s(h) \to 0$.
options.why: $s(h)$ is about $f$, not $F$. $F$ is continuous even at a jump of $f$.

options.text: The strip's area tends to 0.
options.why: The area tends to 0, but we divide it by $h$, which tends to 0 too.

hints.text: Which hypothesis is about values of $f$ near $c$?
Continuity at $c$ gives a $\delta$ for each $\varepsilon$.
For $|h| < \delta$, every $t$ in the strip is within $\delta$ of $c$.

feedback.correct: Right. Continuity at $c$ is exactly what makes $s(h) \to 0$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the hypothesis that controls $|f(t) - f(c)|$ for $t$ near $c$.

explain.text: Continuity at $c$ says $|f(t) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ once $|t - c| < \delta$. Then $s(h) \le \varepsilon$ for $0 < |h| < \delta$. So the quotient tends to $f(c)$, which is $F'(c) = f(c)$.

screens.title: Part one assembled
screens.prose: Part one of the fundamental theorem: if $f$ is integrable on $[a, b]$ and continuous at $c$, then $F(x) = \int_a^x f$ has $F'(c) = f(c)$. One line is flawed, and two lines may come in either order.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Continuity at $c$ gives $\delta > 0$ with $|f(t) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ whenever $|t - c| < \delta$.
For $0 < |h| < \delta$, every $t$ between $c$ and $c + h$ has $|t - c| < \delta$, so the right side is at most $\tfrac{1}{|h|} \cdot \varepsilon|h| = \varepsilon$ in size.
So the difference quotient tends to $f(c)$ as $h \to 0$: $F'(c) = f(c)$. $\blacksquare$
By the mean value theorem, $F(c + h) - F(c) = F'(\xi)\,h$ for some $\xi$.
lines.why: The mean value theorem needs $F$ differentiable, which is the claim. The proof would be circular.

hints.text: Start with the identity for the quotient minus $f(c)$.
Then bring in continuity at $c$, then bound the integral.
Finish with the limit.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The order is: write the identity, fix $\delta$ from continuity, bound, conclude.

byKey.d1: You used the mean value theorem on $F$. That assumes $F'$ exists, which is what we are proving.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: The identity turns the quotient's error into an average of $f(t) - f(c)$ over the strip. Continuity at $c$ makes that average small. Integrability is needed only so that $F$ exists.

screens.title: A moving upper limit
screens.prose: Let $F(x) = \int_0^{x^2} \cos t\,dt$. Write $F(x) = H(x^2)$ with $H(u) = \int_0^u \cos t\,dt$. Part one gives $H'(u) = \cos u$, since $\cos$ is continuous.
screens.question: What is $F'(x)$?

hints.text: Use the chain rule on $H(x^2)$.
$H'(u) = \cos u$ at $u = x^2$, and $\tfrac{d}{dx} x^2 = 2x$.
So $F'(x) = \cos(x^2) \cdot 2x$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Differentiate $H(x^2)$ by the chain rule, with $H' = \cos$.

byKey.nochain: You forgot the chain rule. The upper limit $x^2$ moves at rate $2x$.
byKey.cosx: You put $x$ into $\cos$. The integrand is read at the upper limit $x^2$.
byKey.sin: You integrated $\cos$ again. Part one returns the integrand itself, $\cos$, at $x^2$.

explain.text: $F = H \circ q$ with $q(x) = x^2$, so $F'(x) = H'(x^2)\,q'(x) = 2x\cos(x^2)$. Here $F(x) = \sin(x^2)$ as a check. The upper limit moves at rate $2x$ and the strip there has height $\cos(x^2)$.

screens.title: A jump in the height
screens.prose: Let $f = 0$ on $[0, 1)$ and $f = 1$ on $[1, 2]$. Then $F(x) = \int_0^x f$ is 0 for $x \le 1$ and $x - 1$ for $1 \le x \le 2$.
screens.question: What happens to $F$ at $x = 1$?

options.text: $F$ is continuous at 1 but has a corner: left slope 0, right slope 1, so $F'(1)$ does not exist.
$F$ jumps at 1, as $f$ does.
options.why: You copied the jump of $f$ to $F$. $|F(x) - F(y)| \le |x - y|$ here, so $F$ cannot jump.

options.text: $F'(1) = 1 = f(1)$, by part one.
options.why: Part one needs $f$ continuous at $c$. At 1 it is not, and the left slope is 0.

options.text: $F'(1) = \tfrac12$, the average of the two sides.
options.why: A derivative is not an average of one-sided slopes. When they differ it does not exist.

hints.text: Compute the slopes of $F$ just left and just right of 1.
Left of 1, $F = 0$; right of 1, $F = x - 1$.
Slopes 0 and 1 differ, so there is no single tangent.

feedback.correct: Right. Continuous, with a corner where $f$ jumps.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the left and right difference quotients of $F$ at 1.

explain.text: $F$ is continuous everywhere, since $|f| \le 1$. But $\tfrac{F(1+h) - F(1)}{h}$ is 1 for $h > 0$ and 0 for $h < 0$, so $F'(1)$ does not exist. Part one fails exactly where its hypothesis, continuity at $c$, fails.

screens.title: Part two: evaluating by an antiderivative
screens.prose: Part two: if $G' = f$ on $[a, b]$ and $f$ is integrable, then $\int_a^b f = G(b) - G(a)$. For any partition $P$, the change in $G$ telescopes: $$G(b) - G(a) = \sum_{k=1}^n \big(G(x_k) - G(x_{k-1})\big).$$
screens.question: Which result turns each $G(x_k) - G(x_{k-1})$ into a value of $f$ times $\Delta x_k$?

options.text: The mean value theorem (l18): $G(x_k) - G(x_{k-1}) = G'(c_k)\,\Delta x_k$, which is $f(c_k)\,\Delta x_k$.
Part one, applied to $G$.
options.why: Part one is about $\int_a^x f$ and needs $f$ continuous. Here $f$ is only integrable.

options.text: The definition of the derivative.
options.why: The definition gives $G(x_k) - G(x_{k-1}) \approx f(x_k)\,\Delta x_k$ only, with an error we cannot control.

options.text: Telescoping.
options.why: Telescoping gave the sum. It says nothing about each term.

hints.text: We need an exact equality on each piece, with a point inside it.
$G$ is differentiable on each piece.
The mean value theorem gives $c_k$ with $G'(c_k)\,\Delta x_k$.

feedback.correct: Right. The mean value theorem, once on each piece.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a theorem giving an exact equality with a derivative at an inside point.

explain.text: $G$ is differentiable, so the mean value theorem gives $c_k \in (x_{k-1}, x_k)$ with $G(x_k) - G(x_{k-1}) = f(c_k)\,\Delta x_k$. Summing gives $G(b) - G(a) = \sum_k f(c_k)\,\Delta x_k$. That sum sits between $L(f, P)$ and $U(f, P)$.

screens.title: Part two assembled
screens.prose: Prove part two: if $G' = f$ on $[a, b]$ and $f$ is integrable, then $\int_a^b f = G(b) - G(a)$. One line is flawed, and two lines may come in either order.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: Let $P$ be any partition $a = x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_n = b$.
Telescope: $G(b) - G(a)$ is the sum of $G(x_k) - G(x_{k-1})$ over $k = 1, \dots, n$.
By the mean value theorem, $G(x_k) - G(x_{k-1}) = f(c_k)\,\Delta x_k$ for some $c_k \in (x_{k-1}, x_k)$.
Since $m_k \le f(c_k) \le M_k$, we get $L(f, P) \le G(b) - G(a) \le U(f, P)$.
This holds for every $P$, so $\sup_P L \le G(b) - G(a) \le \inf_P U$. Both ends equal $\int_a^b f$, since $f$ is integrable. $\blacksquare$
By part one, $G(x) = \int_a^x f + C$ for a constant $C$.
lines.why: Part one needs $f$ continuous, and here $f$ is only integrable. The proof never needs $G$ as an integral.

hints.text: Fix a partition first.
Telescope, then apply the mean value theorem on each piece.
Trap the sum between $L$ and $U$, then use every $P$.

feedback.correct: Right. Telescope, mean value theorem, trap, then every partition.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The order is: fix $P$, telescope, mean value theorem, trap between $L$ and $U$, conclude.

byKey.d1: You used part one. It needs $f$ continuous, and part two must work for any integrable $f$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: The mean value theorem makes $G(b) - G(a)$ a sum $\sum f(c_k)\,\Delta x_k$ for each $P$. Every such sum lies between $L(f, P)$ and $U(f, P)$. So the one number $G(b) - G(a)$ is trapped between $\sup L$ and $\inf U$, which are equal.

screens.title: A negative area
screens.prose: Apply part two to $f(x) = \tfrac{1}{x^2}$ on $[-1, 1]$, using $G(x) = -\tfrac1x$, since $G'(x) = \tfrac{1}{x^2}$.
screens.question: What does $G(1) - G(-1)$ give?

hints.text: Subtract: $-1 - 1$.

feedback.correct: Right. The formula gives $-2$, a negative number for a positive function. Something has gone wrong.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Evaluate $G(1)$ and $G(-1)$ carefully, then subtract.

byKey.pos: You trusted the picture and made it positive. The formula itself gives $-2$; the next screen asks why.
byKey.zero: You cancelled by symmetry. $G$ is odd, so $G(1) - G(-1) = 2G(1) = -2$.

explain.text: $G(1) - G(-1) = -1 - 1 = -2$. Yet $f > 0$, so any integral of it would be positive. The formula was applied where its hypotheses fail.

screens.title: Which hypothesis failed
screens.prose: Part two asks for $G' = f$ at every point of $[a, b]$, and for $f$ to be integrable there. Integrable includes bounded.

screens.question: Why does part two not apply to $\tfrac1{x^2}$ on $[-1, 1]$?

options.text: $G' = f$ fails at 0, where neither is defined, and $f$ is unbounded, so it is not integrable.
It does apply; the integral really is $-2$.
options.why: A positive integrand cannot have a negative integral: $L(f, P) \ge 0$ for every $P$.

options.text: $G$ is not continuous at the end point 1.
options.why: $G(x) = -\tfrac1x$ is continuous at 1. The trouble is at 0, inside the interval.

options.text: The interval is too long for the theorem.
options.why: Length is not a hypothesis. On $[-1, -0.5]$ or $[0.5, 1]$ the theorem applies.

hints.text: Check each hypothesis at every point, including $x = 0$.
At 0, $G$ and $f$ are undefined.
And $\tfrac1{x^2}$ exceeds every bound near 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at $x = 0$, inside the interval.

explain.text: At 0 neither $f$ nor $G$ is defined, so $G' = f$ fails there. Near 0, $\tfrac1{x^2}$ exceeds every bound, so no upper sum is finite. Each half has $\int_\delta^1 \tfrac{1}{x^2}\,dx = \tfrac1\delta - 1$, which grows without bound as $\delta \to 0$.

screens.title: Forward rates from discount factors
screens.prose: In rates, the discount factor to time $T$ is $e^{-\int_0^T f(t)\,dt}$, where $f$ is the instantaneous forward curve. Suppose the market's discount factors give $\int_0^T f(t)\,dt = 0.03T + 0.001T^2$, with $T$ in years.
screens.question: What is the forward rate $f(5)$?

hints.text: $f$ is continuous, so part one says $f(T)$ is the derivative of $\int_0^T f$.
Differentiate $0.03T + 0.001T^2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Differentiate the integral in $T$, then evaluate at 5.

byKey.avg: You divided the integral by $T$. That is the average rate to 5 years, 3.5%, not the forward rate at 5.
byKey.integral: You gave the integral itself, 0.175. The forward rate is its slope.

explain.text: Part one gives $f(T) = \tfrac{d}{dT}(0.03T + 0.001T^2) = 0.03 + 0.002T$, so $f(5) = 0.04 = 4\%$. The average rate to 5 years is only 3.5%, since the curve rises. The 5-year discount factor is $e^{-0.175} \approx 0.8395$.

ideas: For integrable $f$ with $|f| \le M$, $F(x) = \int_a^x f$ is continuous: $|F(x) - F(y)| \le M|x - y|$.
Part one: if $f$ is continuous at $c$, $F'(c) = f(c)$. The quotient's error is an average of $f(t) - f(c)$ over the strip. At a jump of $f$, $F$ has a corner.
Part two: let $G' = f$ with $f$ integrable. Telescoping and the mean value theorem trap $G(b) - G(a)$ between every $L(f, P)$ and $U(f, P)$.

formula.name: Fundamental theorem
formula.note: The first where $f$ is continuous; the second when $G' = f$ on all of $[a, b]$ and $f$ is integrable.
